title: The consequences of food and flight efficiency for the timing of natal dispersal in golden eagles
abstract: Permanent emigration from the natal range represents one of the most critical life history transitions in an animal's life and its timing can have long-lasting consequences. While early-life food conditions are known to affect emigration timing, their interplay with the development and expression of movement skills acting on emigration remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of postfledging flight and feeding behaviour on emigration timing in the Alpine population of the golden eagle, Aquila chrysaetos . We used ground-truthed accelerometer data from falconry golden eagles to train a random forest algorithm. Applying the algorithm to accelerometer bursts of wild birds allowed us to allocate each burst to a behaviour and derive time budgets. Then, we quantified individual-specific developmental rates and individual total frequency of both soaring and flapping flight (energy expenditure) and of feeding behaviour (energy intake) over the early postfledging dependency period and assessed their effect on emigration timing (days since fledging). We found that increased postfledging flight efficiency, characterized by the proportion of total time spent soaring versus flapping, was associated with early emigration but not the developmental rates of flight behaviours. These findings suggest that unmeasured environmental factors or innate activity differences rather than individual differences in flight skill development drive emigration timing. Neither frequent feeding nor nestling body condition was associated with characteristics of flight behaviours. Yet, frequent feeding resulted in early emigration. Despite the strong sexual dimorphism in golden eagles, we only found a difference in time spent flapping between sexes. Together, the results suggest that there might be two environmental factors, favourable food availability and suitable soaring conditions that allow for early emigration. Thus, in addition to food availability, the availability of uplifts in the parental territory facilitating soaring flight may represent a pivotal but underappreciated driver for emigration decisions in juvenile soaring birds.

title: Experimental reduction of male wing length reveals benefits of pairing with good fathers
Temporal dynamics of association patterns in Geoffroy's spider monkeys, Ateles geoffroyi: a multiscale approach using temporal multiplex networks
abstract: Collective patterns of sociospatial behaviour are the result of internal and external factors operating at different temporal scales and can give rise to social structures. In species with high degrees of fission–fusion dynamics, individuals can respond to behavioural drivers by joining or departing from subgroups, thereby modulating how often they co-occur in the same subgroups. Their collective patterns of co-occurrence can help us understand how groups respond to their changing environments. We examined association stability (defined as temporal consistency in patterns of co-occurrence in the same subgroup) in a wild group of Geoffroy's spider monkeys, Ateles geoffroyi , over 24 years, to investigate (1) regularities and disruptions that may give insights into the capacity of spider monkey groups (and those of other species with high degrees of fission–fusion dynamics) to persist through time given the social and ecological challenges faced by individuals and (2) how groups with high degrees of fission–fusion dynamics respond to external drivers and the limitations of their responses. Associations were analysed as temporal multiplex networks where each layer represented associations over a given period considering five temporal scales: fortnight, month, season, year and triennium. We used the structural reducibility analysis to detect temporal redundancy (interpreted as consistency) in association patterns and periods of association stability and instability across scales, including a salient drop in stability in the aftermath of two hurricanes. Two association stability metrics based on the similarity between chronologically adjacent layers revealed scale-dependent relations of association stability with demographic and social variables including subgroup size and its variability, certainty in social context and the number of newborn infants. Our results show the usefulness of multilayer networks to analyse social dynamics in species with high degrees of fission–fusion dynamics.

title: Networking the underground: tracking social associations in burrowing mammals using proximity-light-sensor biologgers
abstract: Wild animals often socialize in microhabitats where direct observations are difficult or impossible, limiting the reconstruction of complete social networks and the understanding of variation in social structure. We designed and tested a novel proximity-logging radiocollar (MamTag) in semifossorial Columbian ground squirrels, Urocitellus columbianus , assessing collar effects, comparing collar- and observation-based social networks, and examining association data gathered in otherwise unobservable contexts. We did not detect a significant effect of collars on body mass or reproduction. Observation- and collar-based networks correlated moderately but consistently. Continuous collar data revealed diel shifts in social behaviour and coherent above- and belowground social organization, with individual centrality largely conserved and spatial proximity shaping network structure. Overall, MamTag collars provided reliable, biologically meaningful measures of social associations and a powerful tool for studying social organization in natural environments.

title: Savannah elephant family dynamics: short- and long-term responses to environmental and social changes
abstract: Multilevel societies offer flexibility in short-term association patterns for individual members while retaining valuable long-term relationships with conspecifics. Using a long-term data set on free-ranging African elephants, Loxodonta africana , in Amboseli, Kenya, we illustrate the complexity of decisions about associates in elephant multilevel societies on annual and longer-term timescales, spanning over 50 years. We explore the social dynamics of elephant families and within-family associations in relation to (1) maternal kinship, (2) demographic processes within a family and (3) environmental conditions. Average matrilineal relatedness among adult females (9 or more years of age) within a maintained social unit (family) was estimated from observed pedigrees as 0.146, equivalent to the level of aunt–niece relatedness. As families increased in size through successful reproduction, relatedness declined and females made more individual choices about associates, reducing cohesion among females from the same family. Droughts also reduced family sociability. Matriarchs, defined as the oldest female in a family and its social centre, were a median of 39 years old at the start of their tenure and led their families for almost 20 years. Matriarch death tended to make families less cohesive in the short term but did not consistently lead to family breakdown.

title: Vocalizations shape roost defence outcomes in a solitary bat

Multilayer network analysis of social strategies across the life span in wild vervet monkeys
abstract: Multilayer network analysis offers a powerful framework for studying social systems but remains largely descriptive. We argue that this approach is most informative when guided by explicit biological theory. Using a life history perspective, we examined how social strategies are structured and reorganized across the life span in wild vervet monkeys, Chlorocebus pygerythrus . We focused on the exploration–consolidation dynamic proposed by social development theory. We first quantified age-related patterns in degree, strength and skewness in grooming, spatial association and aggression networks. Across domains and sexes, ego-networks were consistently positively skewed, indicating many weak ties alongside a few strong ones, consistent with stable ‘social bubbles’. However, developmental trajectories differed across domains: grooming skewness increased early in life, spatial skewness decreased during juvenile exploration, and aggression skewness remained relatively stable. These patterns suggest domain-specific routes to a shared structural outcome. Multilayer analyses revealed consistently low redundancy across behavioural domains throughout life, indicating limited overlap in partners across contexts. Spearman correlations showed weak but structured alignment in the two affiliative domains but strong differentiation between grooming and aggression from early life, which weakened during the juvenile period then strengthened again in adulthood. We examined temporal processes using cross-lagged models within and across domains. Within domains, juvenile individuals showed domain-specific and variable feedback between investment and partner number, whereas adulthood was characterized by a consolidation pattern in which increased investment predicted reduced partner number. Cross-domain models showed that at age 2, both social effort and its distribution across partners were coupled between spatial and grooming domains. This coupling weakened by age 7 and disappeared in adulthood. Overall, juvenile life represents a period of cross-domain integration followed by progressive domain-specific consolidation. These findings show how combining life history theory with multilayer and temporal network analyses reveals how social niches are actively constructed across development.

title: Reproductive state shapes female social network position in bottlenose dolphins
Beyond the dyad: higher-order structure within cohesive animal groups can reveal novel patterns of subgroup dynamics
abstract: Revealing the consequences of social structure in animal societies is largely determined by our ability to accurately estimate functionally relevant patterns of social contact among individuals. Of particular relevance are social contacts that drive and maintain the cohesion of moving animal groups. Prior studies have predominantly built up social structure from dyadic connections, which while effective in open societies, where groups are ephemeral and thus less cohesive, may not be sufficient to characterize the fine-grained structure within more cohesive animal groups. This is because associations or interactions can involve more than two individuals participating together, which current approaches cannot distinguish from independent sets of dyadic connections. Here we applied higher-order temporal network approaches to high-resolution GPS data from every group member in two cohesive groups of vulturine guineafowl, Acryllium vulturinum . By quantifying moment-by-moment association dynamics, we revealed clear sex-biased contributions to the group cohesion. Specifically, males form the cohesive core of the group as they participated in temporally consistent subgroups and tended to occupy forward positions in moving subgroups. Females instead remained peripheral and were more likely to leave subgroups, while also occupying rear positions in moving subgroups. These results reveal a likely pathway to leadership that is independent of dominance rank, whereby the cohesion among males, which were previously found to be more likely to lead group movements, results in subgroups that allow them to more often form a majority. Our study thus demonstrates that subgroup association dynamics derived from high-resolution GPS data can provide insights into the fine-scale spatial and social organization of cohesive groups that may shape processes such as collective movement and leadership.
